sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Database persistence is the backbone of every business application, and interviewers use JPA/Hibernate questions to test whether you understand what is happening beneath Spring Data's magic repository methods. The N+1 problem, LazyInitializationException, and @Transactional misuse are the three most cited production bugs in Java applications — freshers who understand them stand out immediately. Knowing the difference between JPA (specification) and Hibernate (implementation) also signals architecture awareness.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
- **ORM** = maps Java class fields to database table columns; you work with objects, the ORM generates SQL
- **JPA** = the specification (javax/jakarta.persistence); **Hibernate** = the most popular JPA implementation
- **EntityManager** = the JPA interface for CRUD operations; Spring wraps this behind JpaRepository
- **Persistence Context** = a first-level cache that tracks entity state within a transaction
- **Entity states** = Transient (new, not tracked) → Persistent (tracked by context) → Detached (was tracked, tx ended) → Removed (marked for delete)
- **@OneToMany / mappedBy** = the `mappedBy` side is NOT the owner; the **owning side** holds the foreign key column
- **LAZY** = load related data only when accessed; **EAGER** = load immediately with the parent query
- **N+1 problem** = 1 query to load N parents, then N queries to load each parent's children — fetch join or @EntityGraph solves it
- **@Transactional** = wraps a method in a database transaction; REQUIRED propagation joins an existing tx or starts a new one

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- `jpa-basics-and-orm-concepts` — drill: ORM benefit, entity states and what triggers each transition, EntityManager vs Spring Data repository
- `entity-mapping-annotations` — drill: @Entity + @Id is minimum, @GeneratedValue strategies (IDENTITY is most common for MySQL/PostgreSQL), @Column nullable/unique
- `jpa-relationships` — drill: @OneToMany with mappedBy on the non-owner side; @ManyToOne on the child is the owning side; cascade ALL vs specific types
- `spring-data-repositories` — drill: JpaRepository extends PagingAndSortingRepository extends CrudRepository; derived query naming rules
- `jpql-and-derived-queries` — drill: JPQL uses entity/field names not table/column names; Pageable for pagination
- `transactions-basics` — drill: @Transactional default propagation = REQUIRED; checked exceptions do NOT trigger rollback by default
- `lazy-vs-eager-loading` — drill: @OneToMany default = LAZY; @ManyToOne default = EAGER; LazyInitializationException = access after tx closed
- `comparisons` — drill: JPA vs Hibernate, JPQL vs SQL, LAZY vs EAGER with N+1 implications
- `scenario-based` — drill: fix LazyInitializationException (open session in view or @EntityGraph or DTO projection), N+1 fix

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- "What is the difference between JPA and Hibernate?" → JPA is the specification; Hibernate is the implementation; Spring Boot auto-configures Hibernate as the JPA provider
- "What is the N+1 problem?" → Loading 100 orders then triggering 100 separate queries for each order's items — fix with JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph
- "What is LazyInitializationException?" → Accessing a LAZY collection after the persistence context (transaction) is closed; fix: extend tx scope, use DTO projection, or @EntityGraph
- "Which side owns a @OneToMany relationship?" → The @ManyToOne side (child, holds the FK column) owns it; @OneToMany with mappedBy is the inverse side
- "What is @Transactional default propagation?" → REQUIRED — joins existing transaction if one exists, starts a new one if not

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"In my Spring Boot projects I use Spring Data JPA with Hibernate as the JPA provider. I annotate entity classes with @Entity and @Id, map relationships with @OneToMany and @ManyToOne, and write queries using derived method names or @Query JPQL. I'm careful about LAZY vs EAGER loading — I keep collections LAZY and use @EntityGraph or JOIN FETCH when I need the related data in a specific query to avoid the N+1 problem. I annotate service methods with @Transactional to ensure that operations run atomically and roll back on failure."*
